summary: Presents a YANG 1.1 module defining identities, typedefs, and groupings useful to cryptographic applications.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9640 defines a reusable set of building blocks for configuring cryptographic material over a network management protocol such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. It names every way a password, key or certificate can be encoded, so that other modules can share one vocabulary instead of each inventing its own.

questions: what is a yang grouping for keys
how does yang store passwords and keys
subtitle: A shared YANG vocabulary for configuring passwords, keys and certificates over NETCONF and RESTCONF.

tldr.problem: Network management protocols have to carry passwords, private keys, symmetric keys, certificates and certificate signing requests, and each of these has several possible encodings. Without a shared model, every module invents its own vocabulary.
tldr.mechanism: The module names each encoding with an identity, gives the encoded bytes a typedef, and provides groupings other modules reuse, with features that let a device advertise which optional encodings it supports.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9640 is a Proposed Standard from October 2024 and has not been obsoleted. It is the base that the later truststore and keystore models build on.

today: RFC 9640 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024 and has not been obsoleted. It defines only groupings, so it is meant to be imported by other modules, such as the truststore and keystore models that build on it.

sections.title: What the Module Provides
sections.content:
RFC 9640 presents a YANG 1.1 module named ietf-crypto-types. YANG is the data modeling language used to describe the configuration and state data that NETCONF and RESTCONF carry, so a module like this one lets a network management client configure passwords, keys and certificates on a device.

The module is a set of building blocks rather than a finished data tree. It defines no data nodes of its own. Other modules import it, use its groupings inside their own trees, and rely on its identities to say which encoding a value uses.

The module fits into a family of documents that together configure the clients and servers of NETCONF and RESTCONF. The truststore and keystore models depend on this one, and the TCP, SSH, TLS, HTTP, NETCONF and RESTCONF client-server models sit above them in that family. The module is compliant with the Network Management Datastore Architecture and defines no protocol-accessible nodes that are config false, so it has no state data of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines a YANG module called ietf-crypto-types. Other modules import it to describe passwords, keys and certificates in a common way, instead of each one inventing its own vocabulary.

sections.title: Features, Identities and Typedefs
sections.content:
The module has three kinds of building block. A feature is an optional capability that a device advertises, so a client can ask before it uses an encoding the device does not support. The module defines 17 features, covering the uncommon key formats, the certificate signing request formats, the certificate expiry notification and the three ways each secret can be held.

An identity is a named constant that other modules can extend. The module defines five base identities: public-key-format, private-key-format, symmetric-key-format, encrypted-value-format and csr-format. The base identities are abstract in the sense that they only name a class of formats, not a specific format. Derived identities name the concrete encodings, such as subject-public-key-info-format, rsa-private-key-format and cms-enveloped-data-format.

A typedef gives a type to the bytes of a well-known structure. Every typedef in the module extends YANG's binary type and encodes an ASN.1 structure using the DER encoding rules. The typedefs cover certificates, certificate revocation lists, OCSP requests and responses, certificate signing requests and the CMS structures.
sections.plainLanguage: The module names optional capabilities, the encodings that keys and certificates can use, and the byte formats of well-known structures. A device advertises which capabilities it has, so a client does not configure something it cannot read.

sections.title: Groupings for Keys, Passwords and Certificates
sections.content:
Twelve groupings hold the reusable sub-trees. A grouping is a template that another module inserts into its own tree with a single statement.

Each secret has a format node that names its encoding and a choice that says how the value is held. A password can be a cleartext-password or an encrypted-password. A symmetric key can be a cleartext-symmetric-key, a hidden-symmetric-key or an encrypted-symmetric-key, and a private key can be a cleartext-private-key, a hidden-private-key or an encrypted-private-key. A hidden value is an empty node, because the real value must not be presented through the management interface at all.

An encrypted value is a container with three parts: encrypted-by, which the module leaves empty for a consuming module to fill with a reference to the encrypting key; encrypted-value-format, which names the encoding of the ciphertext; and encrypted-value, which holds the bytes. A public key is simpler, with only a format node and the key bytes, because there is no reason to hide a public key.

Certificates come in two groupings. A trust anchor certificate holds a chain containing at most one self-signed root certificate. An end-entity certificate holds a chain containing at most one certificate that is neither self-signed nor marked as a certification authority. A certificate-expiration notification lets a server tell clients when a certificate is nearing expiration.
sections.plainLanguage: Each password or key has a node that names its encoding and a choice that says whether the value is written out, hidden, or stored encrypted. An encrypted value also points at the key that encrypted it, which the module using it supplies.

sections.title: The Generate-CSR Action
sections.content:
The generate-csr action asks the device to build a certificate signing request. It takes two input parameters: csr-info, which holds the CertificationRequestInfo structure describing what the certificate should say, and csr-format, which names the requested format. The action returns the request in that format. The only format defined here is p10-csr-format, the PKCS #10 structure defined in RFC 2986.

The action is guarded by the csr-generation feature, and the p10 format by the p10-csr-format feature, so a client can tell whether the device supports it before it tries.

Two groupings tie the action to a key. The asymmetric-key-pair-with-cert-grouping holds one asymmetric key with at most one associated certificate, and the asymmetric-key-pair-with-certs-grouping holds one asymmetric key with a list of certificates. Both let a client request a signing request for a named key and then attach the certificate that comes back.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask the device to build a certificate signing request for one of its keys. The request names the format wanted and returns the signed request, ready to send to a certificate authority.

sections.title: Example Configuration
sections.content:
The RFC shows an example module that uses the groupings, and a configuration that exercises them. It stores one symmetric key as cleartext in the octet-string-key-format and one in the one-symmetric-key-format. It stores an asymmetric key with a hidden private key, another with a cleartext RSA private key, and a third whose RSA private key is encrypted.

The chain of encryption is visible in the data. A hidden asymmetric key encrypts a symmetric key, and that symmetric key encrypts both the RSA private key and the password. Each encrypted value names the key that encrypted it and the format of the ciphertext, so the device can work out how to unwrap it.

The examples use the XML encoding of YANG, but the RFC notes that JSON could be used instead, and that BASE64VALUE= stands in for the base64-encoded binary data, which would otherwise make the examples hard to read.
sections.plainLanguage: The example configuration stores keys in several ways and encrypts one key with another. Each encrypted value names the key that encrypted it, so the device can undo the encryption.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is explicit about the risks. Storing cleartext passwords and keys in the configuration database is NOT RECOMMENDED, and each such option sits behind its own feature so a device can refuse it. Encrypted values use the CMS EncryptedData structure for a symmetric key and the CMS EnvelopedData structure for an asymmetric key, so any encryption algorithm can be used.

When a symmetric key encrypts a password or key, a proper block cipher mode must be used, such as AEAD or CBC, so that a random initialization vector is part of the input. This makes the ciphertext of the same secret differ each time and makes pre-computed tables much harder to build. The Electronic Codebook mode must not be used. Cleartext key values should be zeroized when they are deleted, so that remnants of the storage cannot be read afterwards.

Two design decisions are recorded as deliberate omissions. The Certificate Request Message Format was considered and left out because market demand was unclear, and key generation is not supported: earlier revisions had calls for generating keys, but they were removed because there was no consensus on how to name the key algorithm generically. Keys must be configured by an external client, though protocol-specific modules can define their own key generation calls.

On access control, the module applies the NACM extension default-deny-all to the cleartext password, cleartext symmetric key, cleartext private key and certificate data nodes, and default-deny-write to every node the module defines. The generate-csr action carries default-deny-all as well, and the RFC recommends that implementations assert channel binding so that the request comes from the same application layer that authenticated the secure transport.
sections.plainLanguage: Cleartext secrets in the configuration database are not recommended, and each way of holding a secret has its own feature flag, so a device can refuse it. Encrypted values must use a block cipher mode that hides whether two secrets are the same.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-crypto-types in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as the registrant contact. The same module name ietf-crypto-types is registered in the YANG Module Names registry with the prefix ct and RFC 9640 as its reference.

Those two registrations are what let a client find this module by name and recognise the data it exchanges with a device.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA has registered the module's name and its XML namespace. A client can use the registered name to find the module and the namespace to recognise the data it exchanges with a device.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS A SECRET VALUE CAN BE HELD

items.title: Cleartext
items.text: The value itself is written to the configuration database. The RFC calls this NOT RECOMMENDED.

items.title: Hidden
items.text: An empty node. The value exists on the device but is never sent through the management interface.

items.title: Encrypted
items.text: The ciphertext is stored, together with a reference to the key that encrypted it and the format used.
